title: Early-Onset Accommodative Esotropia: A Clinical Masterclass
summary: A comprehensive guide to the pathophysiology, classification, and management of accommodative esotropia (Acc ET) manifesting in early childhood. This infographic detail the nuances of the Donders Principle, AC/A ratio calculation, and evidence-based treatment protocols for residents and fellows.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Accommodative Esotropia (Acc ET) is defined as a convergent ocular deviation associated with the activation of the accommodation reflex. Early-onset cases typically manifest between 6 months and 3 years of age, though 'early-onset' specifically refers to those occurring before age 1. It is driven by the physiological link between accommodation and convergence (the AC/A ratio) and is the most common cause of childhood esotropia.

rows: Residual ET even with full correction

sections.title: Clinical Features & Signs
content: Sudden or gradual onset of 'crossing'
Initial intermittency (worse with fatigue/near work)
Variable angle of deviation
Diplopia or suppression in older children
Risk of refractive or strabismic amblyopia
Closing one eye in bright light (occasional)

sections.title: Mandatory Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Cycloplegic Refraction (Atropine 1% or Cyclopentolate 1%)
Step 2: Measurement of Deviation (SPCT) at Distance & Near
Step 3: Determination of AC/A Ratio (Gradient or Heterophoria)
Step 4: Assessment of Sensory Status (Stereopsis/Worth 4-Dot)
Step 5: Dilated Fundus Exam to rule out sensory causes

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Is it truly Acc ET?

content.explanation: AC/A = (Deviation with lens - Deviation without lens) / Power of lens. Example: If +3.00 lens changes ET from 30 to 12, AC/A = (30-12)/3 = 6.

sections.title: Management Strategy: Refractive ET
content: 1. Prescribe FULL cycloplegic hyperopic correction
2. Re-evaluate in 4-6 weeks for adaptation
3. Check for residual amblyopia; treat with patching
4. Monitor every 3-6 months for stability
5. Gradual reduction of plus (weaning) only after age 7-8

sections.title: Management: Non-Refractive (High AC/A)
content: 1. Prescribe full distance correction
2. Add +2.50 or +3.00D Bifocals (Executive or Flat-top)
3. Ensure the bifocal line bisects the pupil (high line)
4. If residual ET remains at near, consider surgery
5. Miotics (Phospholine Iodide) rarely used due to side effects

sections.title: RED FLAGS: When it's NOT simple Acc ET
content: Acute onset with headache or vomiting (Intracranial Pressure)
Abduction deficit (6th Nerve Palsy/Duane's)
Leukocoria (Retinoblastoma causing sensory ET)
Incomitance in different gazes
Nystagmus with neurological features

sections.title: Surgical Indications
content: Partially Accommodative ET: Surgery for the NON-accommodative residual component
Decompensated ET: When glasses no longer control the deviation
High AC/A: Surgery (Bi-Medial Recession) if bifocals fail or are unacceptable
Recession is based on the residual angle with full correction

content.explanation: Accommodation (driving force), Amblyopia (primary risk), Anisometropia (frequent association).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Exam Room
content: Always use Atropine for the first refraction in early onset cases to ensure maximal cycloplegia.
Hyperopia in Acc ET is dynamic; it may increase until age 7.
Don't 'cut the plus' in children under 6 years old.
Stereopsis is the best indicator of successful management.

sections.title: Prognosis & Long-Term Outcomes
sections.content: Most children with pure refractive Acc ET achieve excellent binocularity and high-grade stereopsis if treated early. About 10-15% may eventually require surgery for decompensation. Spontaneous resolution occurs in some children as they outgrow hyperopia in their teens.

sections.title: Recent Advances: The PEDIG Evidence
content: PEDIG studies suggest that +2.50 bifocals are generally as effective as +3.00 for High AC/A.
Early full correction significantly reduces the incidence of permanent amblyopia.
Ongoing research into the genetic markers of high hyperopia and Acc ET linkage.
